items.prompt: What is the main reason the whale shark can grow so large?

options.label: It feeds on tiny plankton, which allows it to grow steadily without needing large prey.
options.feedback: Correct. The whale shark filters plankton and small organisms from the water, which are abundant enough to support its huge size.

options.label: It has a very fast metabolism that turns food into growth almost instantly.
options.feedback: Wrong. A fast metabolism would require constant large meals; the whale shark's size comes from filtering vast amounts of tiny food, not from speed.

options.label: It stores fat in its liver like a whale to survive long periods without eating.
options.feedback: Wrong. The whale shark does not store fat like a mammal; it feeds regularly on plankton and small prey.

options.label: It has a swim bladder that lets it float effortlessly, saving energy for growth.
options.feedback: Wrong. The whale shark is a shark, so it has no swim bladder; its large size is supported by water, but its growth comes from feeding on plankton.

items.ok_line: Plankton is plentiful enough to feed a giant.
items.ko_line: Whale sharks are fish, not fat-storing mammals.
items.exp_text: The whale shark grows large because it straines tiny plankton and small organisms from the water with its wide mouth. Plankton is extremely abundant, so it can eat enough to sustain a huge body without chasing fast prey.

items.prompt: What body feature gives the sailfish its sudden bursts of speed?

options.label: Its long, thin tail fin that acts like a rudder.
options.feedback: Wrong. The tail fin helps steer and push, but the speed comes from the powerful muscles and streamlined shape, not the tail fin alone.

options.label: Its large dorsal fin that folds down to reduce drag.
options.feedback: Correct. The sailfish's tall dorsal fin lies flat against its body when it accelerates, cutting water resistance and letting it sprint fast.

options.label: Its gills that pump extra oxygen into the blood during a chase.
options.feedback: Wrong. Gills exchange oxygen, but they do not fold or change shape to speed the fish; the fin is the key feature.

options.label: Its swim bladder that adjusts buoyancy instantly for a quick start.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sailfish, like all billfish, has no swim bladder; its speed comes from its body shape and fin.

items.ok_line: The sailfish tucks its sail to slice through water.
items.ko_line: Speed comes from reduced drag, not the tail fin.
items.exp_text: The sailfish has a tall dorsal fin that normally stands up, but when it chases prey, the fin folds down flat against its back. This makes the fish more streamlined, so it can accelerate suddenly and reach high speeds.

items.prompt: How does a sperm whale cope with the crushing deep-sea pressure?

options.label: Its lungs fill with air to equalize the pressure inside and outside.
options.feedback: Wrong. Filling lungs with air would be dangerous at depth; the sperm whale actually collapses its lungs and relies on stored oxygen in its blood and muscles.

options.label: Its bones are made of extra-dense material that resists compression.
options.feedback: Wrong. Dense bone would make it heavy and hard to dive; the whale's body is compressible, not rigid.

options.label: Its body is flexible and its ribcage can collapse safely.
options.feedback: Correct. The sperm whale's ribcage and lungs are designed to collapse under high pressure, letting its body squeeze without damage as it dives.

options.label: Its skin is covered with a thick layer of blubber that acts as a pressure shield.
options.feedback: Wrong. Blubber insulates and stores energy, but it does not protect against pressure; the whale survives because its body can compress.

items.ok_line: The whale's ribcage folds inward without harm.
items.ko_line: Lungs collapse; pressure is matched by compressible tissues.
items.exp_text: The sperm whale's ribcage and lungs are built to collapse under the immense pressure of deep water. This prevents damage from compression, and the whale uses oxygen stored in its muscles and blood rather than in full lungs.

items.prompt: Why does the Greenland shark live so long?

options.label: It has a special enzyme that repairs all cell damage instantly.
options.feedback: Wrong. No animal repairs all damage instantly; the shark's longevity comes from slow growth and low activity, not from instant repair.

options.label: It hibernates for most of the year, slowing its heartbeat.
options.feedback: Wrong. The Greenland shark does not hibernate; it lives in cold water where its metabolism is naturally slow.

options.label: It produces antifreeze proteins that stop it from aging.
options.feedback: Wrong. Antifreeze proteins help it survive cold water, but they do not stop aging; longevity comes from a slow life.

options.label: It grows very slowly in cold water, which slows its aging process.
options.feedback: Correct. In the frigid Arctic water, the Greenland shark has a very slow metabolism, so it grows slowly and can live for centuries.

items.ok_line: Cold water slows everything down, including aging.
items.ko_line: Longevity comes from slow growth, not cell repair.
items.exp_text: The Greenland shark lives in near-freezing water that keeps its metabolism slow. A slow metabolism means slow growth and slow aging, so the shark can live for over 400 years, one of the longest lifespans of any vertebrate.

items.prompt: Why does the ocean sunfish release so many eggs at once?

options.label: Most of the eggs and young will be eaten by predators, so many are needed.
options.feedback: Correct. The sunfish produces millions of eggs because very few will survive to adulthood; the huge number ensures at least some survive.

options.label: The eggs are very small, so many are needed to make a large baby.
options.feedback: Wrong. Egg size does not determine number; the sunfish produces many eggs because survival is low, not because it needs a large baby.

options.label: The sunfish has no predators as an adult, so it can afford to waste eggs.
options.feedback: Wrong. Adult sunfish are slow and can be preyed on; the huge egg number is a strategy to overcome high death rates in young.

options.label: It lays eggs only once in its life, so it must release all at once.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sunfish spawns repeatedly across its life; the massive release per spawning is about survival odds, not a one-time event.

items.ko_line: Egg number is about survival, not egg size.
items.exp_text: Sea currents carry sunfish eggs into the open ocean, where most larvae are eaten by predators or die from lack of food. Releasing millions of eggs at once gives the species a chance that a few offspring will survive to adulthood.

items.prompt: How does the mantis shrimp deliver such a powerful strike?

options.label: It swings its whole body forward to add weight to the blow.
options.feedback: Wrong. The mantis shrimp does not use body weight; it uses spring-like limbs that snap forward very quickly.

options.label: Its club-like limbs spring forward with extreme speed, creating a shockwave.
options.feedback: Correct. The mantis shrimp's limbs are spring-loaded and move so fast that they even create a collapsing bubble that adds extra force.

options.label: It fires a jet of water at the shell to break it.
options.feedback: Wrong. It uses physical impact from its limbs, not a water jet; the shockwave comes from the fast movement itself.

options.label: It uses poison in its claw to dissolve the shell before striking.
options.feedback: Wrong. The strike is purely mechanical; the shrimp does not use poison to weaken the shell.

items.ko_line: Speed, not mass, does the damage.
items.exp_text: The mantis shrimp keeps its club-like limbs cocked under tension and releases them in a split second. The limb accelerates so fast that it hits the shell with a shockwave, and in some species, a bubble collapses to deliver an extra blow.

items.prompt: Why does the European eel leave the river to swim across the ocean?

options.label: It searches for warmer water to survive the winter.
options.feedback: Wrong. The eel migrates to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, not to escape cold; rivers can be warm enough.

options.label: It must feed on ocean plankton that is absent from rivers.
options.feedback: Wrong. The eel eats small animals in rivers; the migration is for reproduction, not for food.

options.label: It returns to the open ocean to lay its eggs and start a new generation.
options.feedback: Correct. Adult European eels swim thousands of kilometers to the Sargasso Sea, where they spawn, and then die; the young eels later drift back to rivers.

options.label: It flees to avoid predators that live in freshwater.
options.feedback: Wrong. The eel has lived in rivers for years; the migration is a breeding journey, not an escape from danger.

items.ok_line: Rivers are home, but the sea is for spawning.
items.ko_line: The trip is about laying eggs, not feeding.
items.exp_text: The European eel grows up in rivers but, at maturity, swims across the Atlantic to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. After releasing eggs or sperm, the adults die, and the tiny larvae drift on currents back to the coasts.

items.prompt: How can a starfish regrow a whole new animal from just a single severed arm?

options.label: The arm carries its own tiny brain that controls the regrowth.
options.feedback: Wrong. Starfish do not have a brain in each arm; regeneration comes from cells that can rebuild the body, not from a separate brain.

options.label: The arm contains a pair of fins that can swim to a new location.
options.feedback: Wrong. Starfish do not swim; the arm regrows a body while staying in place.

options.label: The arm has a stomach that can feed and support the new animal.
options.feedback: Wrong. Some arms may feed, but the key is that the arm has enough tissue and a part of the central disk to regenerate a full body.

options.label: The arm includes part of the central disk, and that tissue can rebuild the whole body.
options.feedback: Correct. If a severed arm includes a piece of the central disk, that piece contains the cells needed to grow a new mouth, stomach, and other arms.

items.ok_line: A slice of the center is enough to regrow.
items.ko_line: An arm without disk tissue cannot make a new starfish.
items.exp_text: When a starfish loses an arm, it can regrow that arm, but to make a new animal, the arm must carry part of the central disk. That tissue holds the structures needed to form a new mouth and stomach, so it can grow into a complete starfish.

items.prompt: How does pufferfish toxin cause paralysis in a predator?

options.label: It blocks nerve signals from reaching the muscles.
options.feedback: Correct. The toxin prevents nerves from sending messages, so the predator's muscles stop working, including those needed for breathing.

options.label: It destroys the predator's red blood cells.
options.feedback: Wrong. The toxin acts on nerves, not on blood cells; blood cell destruction would cause different symptoms, not immediate paralysis.

options.label: It speeds up the predator's heart until it bursts.
options.feedback: Wrong. The toxin does not speed the heart; it blocks nerve signals, which slows or stops muscle activity.

options.label: It makes the predator's stomach swell and block the airway.
options.feedback: Wrong. The effect is on the nervous system, not on the stomach; paralysis is caused by blocked nerve messages.

items.ok_line: Muscles get no signal, so they stop.
items.ko_line: The toxin targets nerves, not cells.
items.exp_text: Tetrodotoxin from the pufferfish binds to nerve channels and stops them from firing. Without nerve signals, the predator's muscles cannot contract, leading to paralysis and often death by suffocation.

items.prompt: How does the electric eel generate its powerful shock?

options.label: It stores electricity in its bones and releases it on demand.
options.feedback: Wrong. Bones are not electric storage; the eel uses special cells in its body.

options.label: It uses modified muscle cells that act like batteries.
options.feedback: Correct. The electric eel has thousands of specialized cells called electrocytes that produce voltage, like many small batteries linked together.

options.label: It rubs its body against the water to create static electricity.
options.feedback: Wrong. Static from rubbing does not produce a strong shock; the shock comes from internal cells, not friction.

options.label: It uses its gills to convert oxygen into electric charge.
options.feedback: Wrong. Gills exchange gases; the electric organs are separate from gills and made of modified muscle tissue.

items.ok_line: Muscle-like cells stack to make a battery.
items.ko_line: The shock comes from internal cells, not friction.
items.exp_text: The electric eel has a large organ made of many electrocytes, which are flattened cells that can produce voltage. When the eel wants to shock, it fires these cells in unison, creating a strong electric field around its body.
